classification.difficultyReason: Investigates an iterative conjecture for thirty starting values and identifies reusable chains.

questions.mappingNote: Testing the conjecture on specified examples is the closest catalogue match; this task does not ask for a proof.
questions.methodNote: Apply the printed odd/even rule repeatedly; reuse known chain tails and count operations through the first 1.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Investigates an iterative conjecture for thirty starting values and identifies reusable chains.

classification.difficultyReason: Extend the supplied counting definition into divisor-based counting and prime-factor exclusions, recognising and correcting overlap when numerators share both prime factors.

questions.mappingNote: Prime factors determine cancellation in the most advanced part. Earlier parts directly assess common factors and simplest form.
questions.methodNote: Printed question 1 counts irreducible fractions; question 2 groups cancellations by divisor; question 3 excludes numerators sharing prime factors. The denominator-1 endpoint is retained as an unresolved source inconsistency.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Generalises irreducible-fraction counts using divisor grouping and distinct prime factors.

classification.difficultyReason: Use the supplied experimental prompts to discover last-digit and odd-square tens-digit restrictions, then apply those patterns to rule out large candidates.

questions.mappingNote: Evaluating squares and interpreting their digit patterns is the directly assessed skill; examples support the exclusions.
questions.methodNote: Experiment with squares, inspect final digits and final digit pairs, then use the observed restrictions to eliminate numbers. Preserve the source's initial calculator-free selection followed by calculator experimentation.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Investigates square-number endings and uses discovered restrictions to exclude large numbers.

classification.difficultyReason: Cube each possible final digit and record its units digit in the supplied correspondence table.

questions.mappingNote: Evaluating powers is the directly assessed catalogue skill.
questions.methodNote: Experiment with cubes and compare their final digits, retaining correspondence with the original final digit.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Investigate how the final digit determines the final digit of a cube.

classification.difficultyReason: Choose experimental fifth powers, notice the unchanged final digit and generalise the pattern using the preceding final-digit investigations as context.

questions.mappingNote: Evaluating powers supports the requested discovery; no index-law shortcut is needed.
questions.methodNote: Continue the source's experimental comparison of final digits for squares, cubes and fourth powers.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Use experimental calculations to discover a final-digit pattern for fifth powers.

classification.difficultyReason: Systematically subtract successive powers of two, test each remainder for primality, and stop when the powers exceed the number; these are routine linked procedures following the taught demonstration.

questions.mappingNote: Determining which candidate summands are prime is the central assessed skill; evaluating powers of two supports the search.
questions.methodNote: Follow the valid 23 demonstration: subtract successive powers of two and retain only prime differences. The printed 61 demonstration includes composite 57 and is not used as a valid pair.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Search all relevant powers of two and test each remaining summand for primality.

classification.difficultyReason: Organise an exhaustive search, distinguish eliminating a candidate with one prime remainder from proving every remainder composite, and record evidence. The supplied demonstration and search advice scaffold the strategy.

questions.mappingNote: Prime/composite classification is the decisive assessed skill; evaluating powers supplies the systematic candidate list.
questions.methodNote: Systematically subtract powers of two, test whether each remainder is prime, and exhibit a prime remainder to eliminate a candidate. Preserve the supplied factorisation demonstration.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Requires a systematic search, prime/composite testing and exhaustive elimination.

classification.difficultyReason: Identify perpendicular heights and missing lengths, then connect triangle areas through subtraction to obtain the shaded area. Earlier parts explicitly supply the intermediate areas needed.

questions.mappingNote: Composite area is the most advanced directly assessed skill; triangle and rectangle area support the intermediate calculations.
questions.methodNote: Use half base times perpendicular height for triangle areas, then subtract component areas. Part b explicitly uses the area of BAC and the result from part a.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Finds several related triangle areas before subtracting them from the square to determine a shaded quadrilateral.

classification.difficultyReason: Combines square and triangle areas to locate a point that bisects a composite region.

questions.mappingNote: The equal-square grid supplies the triangle dimensions; part c combines a triangle and a square to determine an unknown height.
questions.methodNote: Use square area, triangle area from a perpendicular base and height, and addition or subtraction of component areas.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Combines square and triangle areas to locate a point that bisects a composite region.

classification.difficultyReason: Devise an unscaffolded dividing line by reframing half the figure as a whole square plus a triangle, determine the required endpoint from its area, and prove the resulting partition is equal.

questions.mappingNote: The assessed task combines construction with a composite-area proof, making area-composite-figures the closest primary skill.
questions.methodNote: Use square and triangle areas, then add component areas to prove that each region is half the total. No coordinate or algebraic slope method is required.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Construct an equal-area division and prove it by decomposing the figure into a triangle and a square.

classification.difficultyReason: Apply the specified lattice algorithm: split digit products, sum diagonals with carries, and place the decimal point using the taught rule. Larger grids add repetition rather than new strategic decisions.

questions.mappingNote: All three printed questions explicitly request the demonstrated lattice method. Part a uses a three-by-three lattice; b uses four by three; c uses four by four.
questions.methodNote: Construct the lattice with split tens/units cell products; add diagonals from bottom right, carrying to the next diagonal. Locate the decimal point using the diagonal determined by the factors' decimal points.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Construct decimal multiplication lattices, sum diagonals with carrying and locate the decimal point.

classification.difficultyReason: Explain why successive quotients retain higher place values and remainders reveal digits from lowest to highest, connecting the supplied divisions to a powers-of-four expansion rather than merely executing the algorithm.

questions.mappingNote: The entire unnumbered algorithm and its supplied numerical example are retained with the explanation question. Evaluating powers and expanded notation is the closest available classification; the catalogue has no arbitrary-base-conversion skill.
questions.methodNote: Use place-value expansion in powers of the base and the supplied repeated-division algorithm. Each remainder supplies the next digit from the units place upwards.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Explain how repeated division extracts successive base-four place-value digits.

classification.difficultyReason: Evaluate weighted powers in four different bases; index evaluation is the closest existing classification.

questions.mappingNote: Each part evaluates the source base numeral by its place values, using the same expansion principle for bases 7, 4, 3 and 16.
questions.methodNote: Pages 19–20 explain positional notation as a sum of digit multiples of powers of the base. Page 21 supplies further expanded forms.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Evaluate weighted powers in four different bases; index evaluation is the closest existing classification.

classification.difficultyReason: Evaluate binary place values using powers of 2. This is the closest available classification; the catalogue has no binary-conversion skill.

questions.mappingNote: All five parts directly apply the page-22 binary-to-decimal method. Powers and place-value evaluation provide the closest available taxonomy match.
questions.methodNote: Page 22 converts binary numbers to decimal by multiplying each digit by its power-of-2 place value and adding. Pages 23–24 provide binary arithmetic context.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Evaluate binary place values using powers of 2. This is the closest available classification; the catalogue has no binary-conversion skill.

classification.difficultyReason: Add binary numbers by aligning place values and carrying in base 2; the catalogue has no exact binary-arithmetic skill.

questions.mappingNote: All four parts directly assess the binary addition taught in Example 5 on page 23. Page 22 establishes binary place values, and Example 7 on page 24 reinforces column addition. The selected arithmetic skill is the closest available catalogue match.
questions.methodNote: Use binary place values and right-aligned column addition. As in Example 5, carry to the next column whenever a column total reaches two; a total of three writes 1 and carries 1.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Add binary numbers by aligning place values and carrying in base 2; the catalogue has no exact binary-arithmetic skill.

classification.difficultyReason: Subtract binary numbers in aligned place-value columns, including borrowing across zero digits. This is the closest available arithmetic classification.

questions.mappingNote: Question 4 directly assesses binary column subtraction. The selected catalogue skill is the closest available place-value arithmetic skill; it does not specifically describe binary arithmetic.
questions.methodNote: Page 22 establishes binary place values. Page 23 states that binary subtraction uses the same column arrangement as decimal subtraction; Example 6 demonstrates borrowing and alternative regrouping notation. Page 24 continues binary arithmetic.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Subtract binary numbers in aligned place-value columns, including borrowing across zero digits. This is the closest available arithmetic classification.

classification.difficultyReason: Apply the demonstrated three-addend binary addition procedure, interpreting column totals and propagating base-two carries, including a carry spanning more than one place.

questions.mappingNote: All three parts directly apply the three-addend vertical binary method of Example 7. The closest available classification covers addition of multiple numbers using place value.
questions.methodNote: Page 22 establishes binary place values. Page 23 teaches column addition with base-2 carries; Example 7 on page 24 applies it to three addends.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Add three binary numbers using aligned place-value columns and carrying in base 2. The catalogue skill is the closest arithmetic match.

classification.difficultyReason: Identify a missing addend and calculate it using binary subtraction.

questions.mappingNote: Find the missing addend by subtracting 10100 from 111111 using the binary column method of Example 6, then verify by addition. The catalogue has no binary-arithmetic skill; the closest assessed skill is solving an addition/subtraction word problem.
questions.methodNote: Binary place values are powers of 2. Examples 5–7 use vertically aligned binary addition and subtraction, with carrying or borrowing where needed.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Identify a missing addend and calculate it using binary subtraction.

classification.difficultyReason: Find a missing binary addend by subtraction or bridging to the next binary place value; the catalogue has no binary-specific skill.

questions.mappingNote: The unknown addend is the difference between the binary total 1000 and the known addend 111. This is an inverse addition task; the closest supplied classification is addition and subtraction strategies.
questions.methodNote: Use binary place values and base-2 addition or subtraction, carrying or borrowing between columns as demonstrated in Examples 5–7.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Find a missing binary addend by subtraction or bridging to the next binary place value; the catalogue has no binary-specific skill.
